claims.text: The starting catalyst is an uncoated, near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy containing Cu, Ni, Pd, Pt, and other elements.
Atomic layer deposition can form an ultrathin, conformal CeO2 coating with controlled thickness and uniformity on the alloy catalyst.
Optimizing the CeO2 coating will prevent significant blockage of alloy active sites.
The nanoscale CeO2 layer will provide oxygen-storage and oxygen-release functionality.
The CeO2 layer will form strong metal-oxide interfacial bonds with the underlying multi-principal-element alloy.
The CeO2 overlayer will supply active oxygen species at low temperatures.
Active oxygen supplied by the CeO2 overlayer will enhance CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
The CeO2 overlayer will buffer transient oxygen deficits in the exhaust stream.
The CeO2 overlayer will preferentially adsorb H2O and NO, thereby protecting alloy active sites from poisoning.
Strong bonding at the CeO2-alloy interface will inhibit nanoparticle sintering during thermal cycling.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the CeO2-coated catalyst will have a lower light-off temperature for CO oxidation.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the CeO2-coated catalyst will have a lower light-off temperature for hydrocarbon oxidation.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the CeO2-coated catalyst will provide higher CO and hydrocarbon conversion rates.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the CeO2-coated catalyst will be more resistant to H2O poisoning.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the CeO2-coated catalyst will be more resistant to NO poisoning.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the CeO2-coated catalyst will retain more catalytic activity during prolonged accelerated thermal aging.
Adding the CeO2 coating will improve performance without adding platinum-group metals.
The predicted improvements will apply below 150 °C in mixtures containing CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO and after accelerated thermal-aging cycles.
